questions.stem: Lines $y=2x+3$ and $y=11-2x$ meet at $P$. A new line through $P$ is parallel to the segment from $A(1,2)$ to $B(4,0)$ and meets both coordinate axes at $X$ and $Y$. What is the **area** of triangle $OXY$, where $O$ is the origin?

options.errorPath: Find x-intercept 25/2 correctly but submit this length instead of using both intercepts to form the triangular area.
Use the product of the two intercept lengths without the factor one-half required by the triangle area formula.
Find y-intercept 25/3 correctly but mistake it for the required triangular area.
Calculate the area using the intersection's y-coordinate 7 as the vertical axis intercept, rather than 25/3.
Use the two coordinates of intersection P=(2,7) as perpendicular base and height, giving one-half times 2 times 7.

workedSolutionSteps: Solve $2x+3=11-2x$ to obtain $P=(2,7)$. The segment $AB$ has gradient $\frac{0-2}{4-1}=-\frac{2}{3}$.
The new parallel line is $y-7=-\frac{2}{3}(x-2)$, hence $y=-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{25}{3}$. Its positive intercepts are $x=\frac{25}{2}$ and $y=\frac{25}{3}$.
The triangle formed with the coordinate axes therefore has area $\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{25}{2}\times\frac{25}{3}=\frac{625}{12}$ square units.
questions.provisionalAOFocus: AO3 candidate: derive intersection, gradient from two separate points, construct a new line, then use axis geometry for area.
questions.explicitDifferenceFromRoutineSource: Adds transfer to geometric area calculation rather than four coefficient-rotated one-step values of k.
questions.unverifiedTaughtSubskill: Exact classroom treatment of coordinate-axis geometry, parallel gradients and area from intercepts not independently checked.

questions.stem: A straight line through $A(k,6)$ and $B(2,3)$, with $k<2$, meets the positive coordinate axes at $X$ and $Y$. Triangle $OXY$ has area $15$ square units. Which option gives **every possible value of $k$**?

options.errorPath: Recover the correct square-root discriminant but add 2 to the root-transformation result rather than subtract t from 2.
Correctly solve for the positive auxiliary variable t but report its values instead of returning to k=2-t.
Miscalculate the quadratic discriminant 36−16=20 as 24, producing sqrt6 instead of sqrt5.
Retain only the positive-square-root branch of the quadratic, omitting a second admissible k<2 value.
Forget the constant 3 in t=3±sqrt5 when transforming back to k=2-t.

workedSolutionSteps: Put $t=2-k>0$. The slope of $AB$ is $-\frac{3}{t}$, so its positive x-intercept is $t+2$ and y-intercept is $\frac{3(t+2)}{t}$.
The axis-intercept triangle has area $\frac{1}{2}(t+2)\frac{3(t+2)}{t}=15$, hence $(t+2)^2=10t$ and $t^2-6t+4=0$.
Solve $t=3\pm\sqrt{5}$; both values are positive. Converting back gives the two permitted values $k=2-t=-1\pm\sqrt{5}$.
questions.provisionalAOFocus: AO2/AO3 candidate: create a variable slope/intercept model, translate a geometric area constraint to quadratic roots, preserve two valid domain branches.
questions.explicitDifferenceFromRoutineSource: Requires two-branch geometric parameter reasoning instead of the original one-step perpendicular gradient.
questions.unverifiedTaughtSubskill: Quadratic formula and parameter-dependent axis-intercept area must be independently confirmed as taught.

questions.stem: Two adult tickets and three child tickets cost £40; three adult tickets and two child tickets cost £45. A group must buy **exactly 25 tickets**, including **at least 10 child tickets**, on a maximum budget of **£230**. Let $A$ denote the number of adult tickets. What is the **greatest possible value of $A$**?

options.errorPath: Use only the £230 budget and exactly 25 tickets; sixteen adults leave nine children, which violates the ten-child minimum.
Find sixteen adults and nine children using the budget, but report the nine child tickets and disregard the minimum-child constraint.
Apply an unnecessary extra requirement of at least eleven child tickets and cap adults at fourteen, losing one permitted adult ticket.
Confuse the condition requiring at least ten child tickets with a ten-adult maximum, ignoring the exact feasible optimisation.
Ignore the minimum child count and available budget, and count every one of the twenty-five tickets as an adult ticket.

workedSolutionSteps: Write adult price a and child price c. Solve $2a+3c=40$ and $3a+2c=45$ to obtain $a=11$ and $c=6$ pounds.
Let A be adult-ticket count. Exactly 25 tickets gives children $25-A$. The budget requires $11A+6(25-A)=150+5A\le230$, hence $A\le16$.
At least ten children also requires $25-A\ge10$, so $A\le15$. Fifteen adults and ten children cost £225 and meet both conditions; the maximum is $15$.
questions.provisionalAOFocus: AO3 candidate: infer two unit prices, model an integer count/budget feasible region and maximise under independent constraints.
questions.explicitDifferenceFromRoutineSource: Adds separate child quota and optimisation constraints to the original one-step ticket substitution.
questions.unverifiedTaughtSubskill: Two-variable budget inequalities and integer maximum feasible choices need actual Year9 lesson coverage evidence.

questions.stem: For real parameters $k$ and $t$, consider $\begin{cases}2x+3y=7\\(k+2)x+(2k+1)y=14+t\end{cases}$. In the options, $I$ states when the system has **infinitely many solutions**, and $N$ states when it has **no solution**. Which gives both conditions correctly?

options.errorPath: Interchange the equal and unequal right-hand-side conditions: the consistent proportional case gives infinitely many, not none.
Set the coefficient proportionality at k=3 even though it does not make both rows parallel.
Forget the second constant is 14+t, not t, when matching the triple of the first right-hand side.
Treat the nonsingular cases with k different from four as inconsistent, although they instead have one unique solution.
Exclude inconsistent cases with t below seven, despite every t different from seven producing parallel distinct lines.

workedSolutionSteps: A no-solution or infinitely-many-solution system requires the two coefficient pairs to be proportional: $2(2k+1)-3(k+2)=0$, hence $k=4$.
At $k=4$ the second left-hand side is $6x+9y=3(2x+3y)$, so its constant must equal $3\times7=21$ to describe the same line.
Thus the system has infinitely many solutions exactly when $k=4,t=7$. If $k=4,t\ne7$, the lines are distinct and parallel, so there is no solution; other k values give a unique solution.
questions.provisionalAOFocus: AO2/AO3 candidate: classify the full two-parameter set into unique, parallel-distinct and coincident systems.
questions.explicitDifferenceFromRoutineSource: Requires two independent parameter conditions and a three-way solution classification instead of finding k from one ratio.
questions.unverifiedTaughtSubskill: General linear-system classifications with two parameters and proportional rows need taught subskill verification.
